# Correlation

## Correlation

So far, we've been talking about continuous outcomes as predicted by different **categorical** variables.

But the world is not limited to categorical predictors!

Today, we are going to talk about estimating associations between two continuous variables by examining their **correlation**.



## Correlation

Correlation is a measure of the **linear association** between two continuous variables. 

Is a standardized version of **covariance**.



## Covariance

Covariance is an unstandardized index of the linear relationship between two continuous variables.

$$ s_{xy} = \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^N (x_i - \bar{x}) (y_i - \bar{y}) }{N - 1} $$

::: subpoint
○ $x_i$: an observation of $x$
:::

::: subpoint
○ $\bar{x}$: sample mean of $x$
:::

::: subpoint
○ $y_i$: an observation of $y$
:::

::: subpoint
○ $\bar{y}$: sample mean of $y$
:::

::: subpoint
○ $N$: sample size
:::

*The deviations of each $x_i$ from its mean and the deviations of each $y_i$ from its mean, multiplied together, summed up, and divided by the sample size minus one.*


## Covariance Visually

```{r}
#| echo: false
library(tidyverse)

# ---- Simulate data with an exact, chosen sample correlation -----------------
set.seed(2027)
n  <- 40
zx <- as.numeric(scale(rnorm(n)))
ze <- as.numeric(scale(rnorm(n)))
ze <- as.numeric(scale(resid(lm(ze ~ zx))))   # orthogonal to zx, so cor = rho exactly

make_df <- function(rho) {
  tibble(
    id = 1:n,
    x  = 50 + 10 * zx,
    y  = 50 + 10 * (rho * zx + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * ze)
  )
}

df <- make_df(0.55)   # medium-ish positive correlation

# ---- Style ------------------------------------------------------------------
grey <- "grey25"
cols <- c(pos = "#3F6E94", neg = "#C2623A")
lims <- c(22, 78)

# ---- Pick a handful of points to feature ------------------------------------
mx <- mean(df$x); my <- mean(df$y)
pick <- function(dx, dy) {
  df |> slice_min((x - mx - dx)^2 + (y - my - dy)^2, n = 1) |> pull(id)
}
p1 <- pick( 12,  12)   # above on both
p2 <- pick(-10, -10)   # below on both
p3 <- pick(  6,   4)   # modestly above on both
p4 <- pick(  9, -10)   # the exception: above on x, below on y

# ---- Main plotting function -------------------------------------------------
cov_plot <- function(df, focus = NULL, show_dx = FALSE, show_dy = FALSE,
                     show_rect = FALSE, rect_all = FALSE, means = TRUE,
                     title = NULL, label = TRUE) {

  mx <- mean(df$x); my <- mean(df$y)

  d <- df |>
    mutate(dx = x - mx, dy = y - my,
           sign = if_else(dx * dy >= 0, "pos", "neg"))

  f <- d |> filter(id %in% focus)

  p <- ggplot(d, aes(x, y)) +
    geom_point(color = "grey40", alpha = 0.6, shape = 16, size = 2)

  if (means) {
    p <- p +
      geom_vline(xintercept = mx, color = grey, linewidth = 0.4) +
      geom_hline(yintercept = my, color = grey, linewidth = 0.4) +
      annotate("text", x = mx + 0.8, y = lims[1] + 1, label = "bar(x)",
               parse = TRUE, hjust = 0, color = grey, size = 4.5) +
      annotate("text", x = lims[1] + 0.8, y = my + 2, label = "bar(y)",
               parse = TRUE, hjust = 0, color = grey, size = 4.5)
  }

  # Rectangles: all points, or just the focus points
  if (rect_all || show_rect) {
    r <- if (rect_all) d else f
    p <- p +
      geom_rect(data = r,
                aes(xmin = pmin(x, mx), xmax = pmax(x, mx),
                    ymin = pmin(y, my), ymax = pmax(y, my), fill = sign),
                alpha = if (rect_all) 0.10 else 0.18, inherit.aes = FALSE)
  }

  # Deviation error bars for focus points
  if (nrow(f) > 0) {
    if (show_dx) {
      p <- p + geom_errorbar(data = f,
                             aes(y = y, xmin = pmin(x, mx), xmax = pmax(x, mx),
                                 color = sign),
                             orientation = "y", width = 2.5, linewidth = 0.8,
                             inherit.aes = FALSE)
    }
    if (show_dy) {
      p <- p + geom_errorbar(data = f,
                             aes(x = x, ymin = pmin(y, my), ymax = pmax(y, my),
                                 color = sign),
                             orientation = "x", width = 2.5, linewidth = 0.8,
                             inherit.aes = FALSE)
    }
    p <- p + geom_point(data = f, aes(color = sign), shape = 16, size = 3.8)

    # Labels only when a single point is featured
    if (label && nrow(f) == 1) {
      if (show_dx) {
        p <- p + annotate("text", x = (f$x + mx) / 2, y = f$y + 2.5,
                          label = "x[i] - bar(x)", parse = TRUE,
                          color = cols[[f$sign]], size = 4.5)
      }
      if (show_dy) {
        p <- p + annotate("text", x = f$x + 1.2, y = (f$y + my) / 2,
                          label = "y[i] - bar(y)", parse = TRUE, hjust = 0,
                          color = cols[[f$sign]], size = 4.5)
      }
    }
  }

  p +
    scale_color_manual(values = cols) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = cols) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(30, 70, 20)) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(30, 70, 20)) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = lims, ylim = lims) +
    labs(x = "X", y = "Y", title = title) +
    guides(x = guide_axis(cap = TRUE), y = guide_axis(cap = TRUE),
           color = "none", fill = "none") +
    theme_classic() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 11))
}
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| echo: false
cov_plot(df, means = FALSE)
```

## Covariance Visually

Examples of positive, zero, and negative covariance:

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 3
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-align: center
#| echo: false
panel <- function(rho, title) {
  d <- make_df(rho)
  feat <- d |> slice_max(abs(x - mean(x)), n = 6) |> pull(id)
  cov_plot(d, focus = feat, show_dx = TRUE, show_dy = TRUE, title = title)
}
panel( 0.6, "Positive: bars mostly have same sign")
panel(-0.6, "Negative: bars mostly have different signs")
panel( 0.0, "Zero: no consistent pattern")
```



## Correlation

It's tricky to numerically interpret a covariance, because it is in a combination of x and y's units. Correlation standardizes covariance down to a single scale.

$$ r_{xy} = \frac{s_{xy}}{s_{x} s_{y}}  $$

::: subpoint
○ $s_{xy}$: covariance between $x$ and $y$
:::

::: subpoint
○ $s_x$: sample standard deviation of $x$
:::

::: subpoint
○ $s_y$: sample standard deviation of $y$
:::

We standardize covariance into correlation just by dividing by the two variables' standard deviations!


## Correlation

It's tricky to numerically interpret a covariance, because it is in a combination of x and y's units. Correlation standardizes covariance down to a single scale.

$$ r_{xy} = \frac{s_{xy}}{s_{x} s_{y}} = \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^N (x_i - \bar{x}) (y_i - \bar{y}) }{\sqrt{\sum_{i = 1}^N (x_i - \bar{x})^2} \sqrt{\sum_{i = 1}^N (y_i - \bar{y})^2}}$$
Bounded from $[-1, \ 1]$

::: subpoint
○ $r_{xy} = -1$: strong negative correlation (when $x$ increases, $y$ tends to decrease)
:::

::: subpoint
○ $r_{xy} = 0$: no correlation ($x$ increasing doesn't provide information about $y$)
:::

::: subpoint
○ $r_{xy} = 1$: strong positive correlation (when $x$ increases, $y$ tends to increase)
:::


## Covariance in R

`cov(x, y = NULL, use = "everything", method = "pearson")`

::: subpoint
○ `x` = numeric vector or dataframe
:::

::: subpoint
○ `y` = if `x` is a numeric vector, can specify `y` as a numeric vector
:::

::: subpoint
○ `use` = how to handle missing (`NA`) values
:::

::: subpoint
○ `method` = which type of coefficient to compute
:::


## Covariance in R

Need to `select()` down just to variables of interest.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}
```{r}
library(palmerpenguins)

penguins |>
  select(flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g) |>
  cov()
```
:::

::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}
```{r}
penguins |>
  select(flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g) |>
  cov(use = "complete.obs")
```
:::
::::


## Correlation in R

`cor(x, y = NULL, use = "everything", method = "pearson")`

::: subpoint
○ `x` = numeric vector or dataframe
:::

::: subpoint
○ `y` = if `x` is a numeric vector, can specify `y` as a numeric vector
:::

::: subpoint
○ `use` = how to handle missing (`NA`) values
:::

::: subpoint
○ `method` = which type of coefficient to compute
:::


## Correlation in R

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
penguins |>
  select(flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g) |>
  cor()
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
penguins |>
  select(flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g) |>
  cor(use = "complete.obs")
```
:::
::::


## Handling `NA`s

`cov()` and `cor()` have different options for what to do if missing values (`NA`s) are present

::: subpoint
○ `"everything"` = use all values: if one is `NA`, result will be `NA`
:::

::: subpoint
○ `"all.obs"` = use all values: if one is `NA` throw an error
:::

::: subpoint
○ `"complete.obs"` = delete rows with any `NA` values at all: if no rows remaining, throw an error
:::

::: subpoint
○ `"na.or.complete"` = delete rows with any `NA` values at all: if no rows remaining, result will be `NA`
:::

::: subpoint
○ `"pairwise.complete.obs"` = for each pair of variables, delete rows if either of the pairs is `NA`: may result in correlations being computed on different sample sizes
:::


## Handling `NA`s

:::: {.columns style="font-size:90%"}
::: {.column width="33%"}
```{r}
penguins |>
  select(flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g) |>
  cor(use = "everything")
```
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
```{r}
#| error: true
penguins |>
  select(flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g) |>
  cor(use = "all.obs")
```
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
```{r}
penguins |>
  select(flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g) |>
  cor(use = "complete.obs")

```
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
```{r}
penguins |>
```

## Ordinal Correlations

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
penguins_ordinal <- penguins |>
  mutate(
    across(
      c(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm),
      function(bill_column) case_when(
        bill_column < quantile(bill_column, .33, na.rm = T) ~ "low",
        between(
          bill_column, 
          quantile(bill_column, 1/3, na.rm = T), 
          quantile(bill_column, 2/3, na.rm = T)
        ) ~ "med",
        bill_column > quantile(bill_column, .66, na.rm = T) ~ "high"
      ) |>
        factor(levels = c("low", "med", "high"), ordered = TRUE),
      .names = "{.col}_ordinal"
    )
  ) |>
  select(ends_with("_ordinal"))

head(penguins_ordinal)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
penguins_ordinal |>
  count(bill_length_mm_ordinal, bill_depth_mm_ordinal)
```
:::
::::


## Ordinal Correlations

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
penguins_ordinal |>
  mutate(across(everything(), as.numeric)) |>
  cor(use = "complete.obs",
      method = "spearman")
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
penguins_ordinal |>
  mutate(across(everything(), as.numeric)) |>
  cor(use = "complete.obs",
      method = "kendall")
```
:::
::::

## Scatterplots

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
If there are lots of datapoints, may want to take down the `alpha` for clearer results.

E.g., with the `tidyverse` `diamonds` dataset.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {.panel-tabset}
### Plot
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-align: center
diamonds |>
  ggplot(aes(x = carat, y = price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.025, shape = 16, size = 2) +
  labs(y = "Price", x = "Carat") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_currency()) +
  guides(x = guide_axis(cap = T),
         y = guide_axis(cap = T)) +
  theme_classic()
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-align: center
r <- cor(penguins$flipper_length_mm, penguins$body_mass_g, use = "complete.obs")

penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point() +
  annotate(geom = "text", label = round(r, 2), x = mean(penguins$flipper_length_mm, na.rm = T),
           y = max(penguins$body_mass_g, na.rm = T)) +
  labs(y = "Body Mass", x = "Flipper Length") +
  guides(x = guide_axis(cap = T),
         y = guide_axis(cap = T)) +
  theme_classic()
```

## Scatterplots

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
Adding a **regression line**.

Defines the relationship between the variables as $y = mx + b$

::: subpoint-narrow
○ $b$: intercept, $y$ when $x = 0$
:::

::: subpoint-narrow
○ $m$: slope, change in $y$ with unit increase in $x$
:::

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.panel-tabset}
### Plot
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-align: center
r <- cor(penguins$flipper_length_mm, penguins$body_mass_g, use = "complete.obs")
r_label <- paste("italic(r) ==", round(r, 2))

penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "seagreen", fill = "seagreen") +
  annotate(geom = "text", label = r_label, x = mean(penguins$flipper_length_mm, na.rm = T),
           y = max(penguins$body_mass_g, na.rm = T), parse = T) +
  labs(y = "Body Mass", x = "Flipper Length") +
  guides(x = guide_axis(cap = T),
         y = guide_axis(cap = T)) +
  theme_classic()
```

### Code

# Simple Regression

## Simple Regression

When we added trendlines (`method = "lm"`) onto our scatterplots, we were performing a **regression**.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="75%"}

::: {.panel-tabset}
### Plot
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-align: center
set.seed(1)

tibble(
  x = rnorm(100, 5, 1.5),
  y = 3 + 2 * x + rnorm(100, 0, 3)
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 10, by = 2), limits = c(0, 10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 25, by = 5), limits = c(0, 25)) +
  guides(x = guide_axis(cap = T),
         y = guide_axis(cap = T)) +
  theme_classic()
```

### Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
set.seed(1)

tibble(
  x = rnorm(100, 5, 1.5),
  y = 3 + 2 * x + rnorm(100, 0, 3)
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 10, by = 2), limits = c(0, 10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 25, by = 5), limits = c(0, 25)) +

```
:::

:::

::: {.column width="75%"}
We are representing the relationship between the variables as $y = mx + b$.

::: subpoint-narrow

:::

## Simple Regression

When we added trendlines (`method = "lm"`) onto our scatterplots, we were performing a **regression**.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="75%"}

::: {.panel-tabset}
### Plot
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-align: center
set.seed(1)

d <- tibble(
  x = rnorm(100, 5, 1.5),
  y = 3 + 2 * x + rnorm(100, 0, 3)
)

fit <- lm(y ~ x, data = d)
b0  <- coef(fit)[[1]]
b1  <- coef(fit)[[2]]

grey <- "grey25"
arr  <- arrow(length = unit(0.09, "inches"), type = "closed")

# One-unit run (x = 8 to 9) and the corresponding rise
x0 <- 7
x1 <- 8
y0 <- b0 + b1 * x0
y1 <- b0 + b1 * x1

ggplot(d, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, shape = 16, size = 1.8, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_abline(intercept = b0, slope = b1, color = "pink3", linewidth = 0.8) +
  
  # Intercept: point where the line crosses x = 0, with a curved arrow and label
  annotate("point", x = 0, y = b0, color = "black", size = 3) +
  annotate("curve", x = 1.6, xend = 0.15, y = b0 + 6, yend = b0 + 0.5,
           curvature = 0.35, arrow = arr, color = grey, linewidth = 0.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.7, y = b0 + 6.8, hjust = 0, color = grey, size = 4.5,
           parse = TRUE, label = sprintf("beta[0] == %.2f", b0)) +
  
  # Slope: one-unit run, then the rise over that run
  annotate("segment", x = x0, xend = x1, y = y0, yend = y0,
           linetype = "dashed", color = grey, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_errorbar(data = tibble(x = x1 + 0.12, ymin = y0, ymax = y1),
                aes(x = x, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax),
                width = 0.15, color = grey, linewidth = 0.6,
                inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  annotate("text", x = x1 + 0.3, y = (y0 + y1) / 2, hjust = 0, color = grey,
           size = 4.5, parse = TRUE, label = sprintf("beta[1] == %.2f", b1)) +
  
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 10, by = 2), limits = c(0, 10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 25, by = 5), limits = c(0, 25)) +
  guides(x = guide_axis(cap = TRUE),
         y = guide_axis(cap = TRUE)) +
  theme_classic()
```

### Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
set.seed(1)

d <- tibble(
  x = rnorm(100, 5, 1.5),
  y = 3 + 2 * x + rnorm(100, 0, 3)
)

fit <- lm(y ~ x, data = d)
b0  <- coef(fit)[[1]]
b1  <- coef(fit)[[2]]

grey <- "grey25"
arr  <- arrow(length = unit(0.09, "inches"), type = "closed")

# One-unit run (x = 8 to 9) and the corresponding rise
x0 <- 7
x1 <- 8
y0 <- b0 + b1 * x0
y1 <- b0 + b1 * x1

ggplot(d, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, shape = 16, size = 1.8, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_abline(intercept = b0, slope = b1, color = "pink3", linewidth = 0.8) +
  
  # Intercept: point where the line crosses x = 0, with a curved arrow and label
  annotate("point", x = 0, y = b0, color = "black", size = 3) +
  annotate("curve", x = 1.6, xend = 0.15, y = b0 + 6, yend = b0 + 0.5,
           curvature = 0.35, arrow = arr, color = grey, linewidth = 0.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.7, y = b0 + 6.8, hjust = 0, color = grey, size = 4.5,
           parse = TRUE, label = sprintf("beta[0] == %.2f", b0)) +
  
  # Slope: one-unit run, then the rise over that run
  annotate("segment", x = x0, xend = x1, y = y0, yend = y0,
           linetype = "dashed", color = grey, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_errorbar(data = tibble(x = x1 + 0.12, ymin = y0, ymax = y1),
                aes(x = x, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax),
                width = 0.15, color = grey, linewidth = 0.6,
                inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  annotate("text", x = x1 + 0.3, y = (y0 + y1) / 2, hjust = 0, color = grey,
           size = 4.5, parse = TRUE, label = sprintf("beta[1] == %.2f", b1)) +
  
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 10, by = 2), limits = c(0, 10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 25, by = 5), limits = c(0, 25)) +
  guides(x = guide_axis(cap = TRUE),
         y = guide_axis(cap = TRUE)) +
  theme_classic()
```
:::

:::

::: {.column width="75%"}
We are representing the relationship between the variables as $y = mx + b$.

::: subpoint-narrow
○ $b$: intercept, $y$ when $x = 0$
:::

::: subpoint-narrow
○ $m$: slope, change in $y$ with unit increase in $x$
:::

In modeling, you more often see this as $y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$

::: subpoint-narrow
○ General linear model
:::

:::
::::


## Regression Example

Let's regress penguin bill length ($x$) on penguin bill depth ($y$). 

$$\text{bill depth}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{bill length}_i + \epsilon_i$$

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
bill_model <- lm(bill_depth_mm ~ bill_length_mm, data = penguins)
summary(bill_model)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
$R^2 = \frac{\mathrm{SS}_\mathrm{regression}}{\mathrm{SS}_y} = \frac{\sum(\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})}{\sum(\hat{y}_i- \bar{y})}$

::: subpoint-narrow
○ Proportion of variance in $y$ explained by the model (predicted values $\hat{y}$)
:::

:::
::::


## `lm()` Objects

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
bill_model_tidy <- broom::tidy(bill_model)
bill_model_tidy
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
bill_model |>
  gtsummary::tbl_regression(intercept = T)
```

:::
::::



:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
Coefficients 

```{r}
coefficients(bill_model)

coefficients(bill_model)[1]
```

:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
Residual variance

```{r}
sigma(bill_model)
```

:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
```{r}
summary(bill_model)$r.squared

summary(bill_model)$adj.r.squared
```

:::
::::


## Regression Interpretation

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
summary(bill_model)
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Intercept**: The expected value of bill depth when bill length is zero is `r coefficients(bill_model)[[1]] |> round(2)`.

::: {.subpoint-narrow .fragment}
○ Do we even care about bill length being zero? 🤔
:::

**Slope**: The expected increase in bill depth with a one unit increase in bill length is `r coefficients(bill_model)[[1]] |> round(2)`.
:::
::::


## Standardizing Variables

We can convert the variables to *z*-scores. Now, $\text{bill length} = 0$ means the *average* bill length across penguins.

```{r}
penguins_cleaned <- penguins |>
  mutate(across(c(starts_with("bill_")), scale, .names = "{.col}_z"))
penguins_cleaned |>
  select(starts_with("bill_"))
```


## Standardized Regression

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="66%"}
```{r}
options(scipen = 999)
bill_model_z <- lm(bill_depth_mm_z ~ bill_length_mm_z, data = penguins_cleaned)
broom::tidy(bill_model_z) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), function(x) round(x, 3)))
```
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
```{r}
cor(
  penguins_cleaned$bill_length_mm,
  penguins_cleaned$bill_depth_mm,
  use = "complete.obs"
)
```
:::
::::

[Simple regression slope coefficient is just the correlation!]{.fragment fragment-index=1}
